Chapter 3: Wrestling with Tradition, Doubt, and Community
As the year went on, the experimenter found herself pulled into some pretty deep questions—about tradition, about doubt, and about the real power of community. The more she tried to live out what the Bible said, the more she realized that “biblical womanhood” isn’t just written on a page. It’s shaped by the people and cultures who interpret it, day after day.
One thing that really stood out was just how tied the Bible’s teachings about women are to their own place and time. Take head coverings—back then, they made sense. What you wore signaled your social standing, even your religious identity. But today? It can feel awkward, maybe even isolating, to try to follow those same rules.
To get a better sense of what this looks like in real life, she reached out to women from all kinds of backgrounds—Orthodox Jews, Amish homemakers, Catholic nuns, and more. Every woman had her own way of living out these ancient texts. Some wore head coverings as a sign of faith. Others thought those traditions were outdated. There were women who embraced traditional roles with joy, and others who found them limiting or even painful.
There was one moment that really stuck—a group of women around a kitchen table, swapping stories about faith and doubt. There was laughter, there were disagreements, but also this strong feeling of solidarity. It’s amazing, isn’t it? Most of us don’t even realize how much our beliefs are shaped by the communities we grow up in, until we step outside those boundaries and really look around.
Of course, the experiment wasn’t always easy. Trying to follow every instruction about purity and menstruation meant spending time apart from loved ones. In ancient days, those practices were supposed to protect and honor. But in a modern home, they just felt lonely and strange. And yet, even then, there was a quiet sense of connection—to women across history who’d faced the same challenges.
Doubt became a constant companion. There were days she wondered if any of this even mattered—was she just playing a game, or was there something deeper waiting on the other side? Conversations with friends and mentors helped her see that faith isn’t about having all the answers. It’s about being brave enough to keep asking the hard questions.
Community turned out to be absolutely essential. Whether at church, at home, or online, there were people who listened, challenged her, and shared their own stories. That’s when it hit her—faith isn’t something you do by yourself. Wrestling with tradition and doubt only makes sense when you have others by your side. That’s what makes it bearable, and sometimes even beautiful.
By the end of this phase, the experimenter learned to welcome both the comfort and the discomfort of tradition. The Bible’s instructions weren’t a burden she had to carry alone. They became an invitation—a chance to join a long, messy, and very human conversation about what it really means to live well.
